sections.h2: Will a fast sale work for a Pasadena home?
sections.html:
Yes. Southeastern Harris County is home to Pasadena, where houses change hands through cash offers, investor purchases and agent listings alike. Closings go fastest for sellers who arrive with the deed, a mortgage payoff figure and a tax certificate in hand before signing the contract.

Rarely is the buyer the bottleneck. Delays come from title defects, an unpaid tax year, a tenant or heirs who cannot agree. Because the county is huge, give the title company your complete legal description and the account number printed on your tax statement from day one, so your lot is never confused with a similar address.

Pasadena is an industrial suburb with a farming past. John H. Burnett of Galveston founded it in 1893, a rail line followed in 1894, and after the 1900 Galveston hurricane the area became a strawberry center. Ship channel industries then reshaped the economy, and today jobs are tied to refineries, the Bayport industrial district and the Johnson Space Center in nearby Clear Lake.

The city covers 58.6 square miles, and the school district has been independent since 1899. Buyers weigh commute, schools and employers, so mention which of those a house sits close to. San Jacinto College and Texas Chiropractic College are in town, and the Pasadena Rodeo and the San Jacinto Strawberry Festival are the big local events.

Values come from the Harris Central Appraisal District. Collection on a Pasadena home belongs to the Harris County Tax Office, which bills the other units on your statement too. January 1 is the valuation date, and each taxing unit picks its own rate.

A statement is due on receipt, and paying by January 31 of the following year avoids penalty and interest. Obtain a fresh statement from the tax office before accepting an offer, so the contract figure agrees with county records.

Confirm every date with the county office first.

Harris County property tax rules for late payers
TopicWhat applies
Timely paymentDue by January 31 of the following year
First late month6% penalty and 1% interest for February
Homestead installment plans12 to 36 months available
Plan start for current-year delinquencyFirst business day in February
Referral to a collection law firmAdditional 15% to 20% penalty on the balance
Tax salesHeld by the eight county constables

Unpaid taxes can be settled from your closing proceeds, so being behind does not by itself stop a sale. It does enlarge the payoff, which is why you should request a figure dated for closing day.

Once taxes go delinquent, an owner with a homestead can sign an installment agreement at any point. Current-year agreements open the first business day of February, and requests arrive after January 31 and before March 1, with the 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest assessed for February.

  • Homestead plans run from 12 months up to 36 months.
  • A deferral can protect the amount owed, but interest of 5 percent per year is added for each year taxes stay delinquent.
  • Online and phone payments count if completed by 11:59 p.m. on or before the due date.
  • Mail must be postmarked on or before the due date.

Someone about to move can lean on a plan for breathing room and clear the balance from closing proceeds.

A tax certificate from the title company shows what has been paid, and any gap is subtracted from your proceeds. Watch one timing trap: a closing between November 15 and January 31 when your mortgage escrows taxes. Phone the lender as soon as the date is fixed so the bill gets paid and the certificate comes back clean.

  • Tell the title company if the lender paid this year's bill from escrow.
  • Ask for any escrow balance back after the payoff.
  • If you claimed a homestead exemption and then sold, the county asks you to correct the account.

A lien stays on the property while taxes are unpaid, so the buyer cannot get clear title until they are.

Part of what the next owner pays is decided by exemptions. Each school district has to give a $140,000 homestead exemption, with another $60,000 for seniors and disabled owners.

  • A homestead's taxable value may climb no faster than 10 percent a year.
  • A disabled veteran may get $5,000 to $12,000 off by rating, and a 100 percent rating can mean a full exemption.
  • If you never claimed the exemption, a buyer late in the year may still claim it for what is left of that year.

Several taxing units can appear on one Pasadena bill, so go through every line.

You can still sell in either case, though each follows its own Texas procedure.

  • Tenant. Eviction starts with written notice to vacate and a justice court case. A writ of possession is available six days after a final judgment. A buyer will ask for the lease and deposit details.
  • Tax judgment. The eight constables hold tax sales for property taken to judgment. Buyers take the property as is, and sales are final.
  • Collection firm. Accounts sent to a law firm face a further 15 to 20 percent penalty.

Paying the tax before judgment leaves more of your proceeds intact. Ask the county for a payoff figure.

sections.h2: Choosing between cash and a listing
sections.html:
Listing may bring a higher price, though commissions, showings and a buyer's lender come with it. Selling for cash gives up part of the price for certainty: the closing date is yours, repairs are not demanded and a loan cannot collapse.

Deferred maintenance or back taxes point toward a cash buyer. A move-in-ready house on a quiet street might do better on the open market. Obtain a written cash offer and a listing estimate, deduct repairs, commissions and carrying costs from the listing figure, then see which is bigger.

sections.h2: Questions to put to each buyer
sections.html:
Ask who covers the title policy, how many days closing takes and whether the price can shift after a walkthrough. Request proof of funds, and learn how much earnest money is deposited and when it comes back to you. Be cautious about anyone who asks for a fee before making an offer or will not commit terms to paper.

If the house is tied up with a tenant, a lien or heirs, say so at the start. Buyers who hear about a problem late tend to cut their offer.

Start a folder now: deed, latest tax bill, name and phone of whoever services your mortgage, any lease. Add court or estate papers if an owner has died, since a buyer must see who is allowed to sign.

When you say yes to an offer, the title company hunts for liens, requests the tax certificate and books the signing. Whatever you owe on the loan or in taxes is taken from the price, and the rest reaches you once the deed is recorded. Because cash skips the lender's appraisal and approval, fewer pieces can push the date back.

Rank offers by what lands in your account, and get the price, closing date and cost split written down by each buyer.

faqs.q: Which county bills Pasadena property tax?
faqs.a: Harris County, through its tax office, while the Harris Central Appraisal District handles values. Request a payoff and a certificate ahead of closing.

faqs.q: Must I clear delinquent taxes before selling?
faqs.a: No, the balance can come from your proceeds at closing. Penalty and interest keep growing, so ask for a total dated for closing day.

faqs.q: When is the county's tax deadline?
faqs.a: January 31 of the year following the tax year. Pay by then and nothing extra is added.

faqs.q: What happens to my escrow if I sell in winter?
faqs.a: The lender may already have paid the bill. Tell it the closing date quickly and ask for any leftover balance once the loan is paid off.

faqs.q: Can I sell with a tenant in place?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer inherits the lease unless you first go through the Texas notice and court steps to empty the house.
